diagram_name: Reinforcing or Balancing? Loops From Ephesus to the Staff Room
chapter_title: Paul at Ephesus, Part 2: Ideas, Legacy, and Lessons in Leading Change
learning_objective: The learner will differentiate reinforcing from balancing feedback loops by counting the minus signs around each of six causal loops, two from Paul's world and four from school change, classifying at least 5 of 6 correctly on the first attempt.
specification:
Type: causal-loop **sim-id:** loops-ephesus-to-staff-room
**Library:** vis-network
**Status:** Specified
**Template:** https://github.com/dmccreary/systems-thinking/tree/main/docs/sims/cld-creation-workflow
**Bloom Level:** Analyze
**Bloom Verb:** differentiate
**Learning Objective:** The learner will differentiate reinforcing from balancing feedback loops by counting the minus signs around each of six causal loops, two from Paul's world and four from school change, classifying at least 5 of 6 correctly on the first attempt. **Prerequisites:** systems thinking, feedback loop, reinforcing and balancing loops, the counting rule, one body many parts, the economics of resistance, the implementation dip, change fatigue (all defined in the chapter above this block). **Evidence of Mastery:** For each of 6 loops, the learner selects Reinforcing or Balancing and submits it. A selection is correct when it matches the "Correct type" column in Content. Mastery is 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Hovering over a link to read its meaning is exploration, not evidence. **Misconceptions:** (1) Reinforcing means good and balancing means bad; loops 3 and 6 are harmful reinforcing loops. (2) Any loop with a minus sign is balancing; loops 3 and 6 each have two minus signs and are reinforcing. (3) The number of variables decides the type. **Instructional Rationale:** Applying the counting rule to concrete loops makes the learner read each link's sign rather than judge by how the variables sound. Mixing ancient and modern loops shows that the structure, not the setting, decides the behavior. **Content:** The rule shown: count the minus signs around the loop; even (including zero) is Reinforcing, odd is Balancing. Convention: the sign after a variable is the sign of the link from that variable to the next; the last variable links back to the first. Six loops, in this order: | # | Setting | Loop (variable, sign of the link to the next) | Minus signs | Correct type | Why (shown as feedback) | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | 1 | School | Student results (+) → Teacher confidence (+) → Quality of use (+) → Student results | 0 | Reinforcing | Zero minus signs is even: success feeds itself. | | 2 | School | Rollout speed (+) → Teacher overload (+) → Resistance (−) → Rollout speed | 1 | Balancing | One minus sign is odd: pushing faster raises resistance that slows the rollout. | | 3 | School | New initiatives launched (+) → Change fatigue (−) → Effort on each initiative (+) → Student results (−) → New initiatives launched | 2 | Reinforcing | Two minus signs is even: weak results prompt more initiatives, which deepen fatigue and weaken results further. | | 4 | Ephesus | Converts to Paul's message (−) → Sales of silver shrines (−) → Silversmiths' opposition (−) → Converts to Paul's message | 3 | Balancing | Three minus signs is odd: growth of the movement provokes opposition that holds it back. | | 5 | Corinth | Honor given to weaker members (+) → Sense of belonging (+) → Members' care for one another (+) → Honor given to weaker members | 0 | Reinforcing | Zero minus signs is even: Paul's body picture describes care that grows on itself. | | 6 | School | Pressure for quick results (+) → Teachers' fear of mistakes (−) → Practice with the new method (+) → Student results (−) → Pressure for quick results | 2 | Reinforcing | Two minus signs is even: during an implementation dip, pressure causes fear, fear cuts practice, and lower results bring more pressure. | Link meanings shown on hover, one per link: loop 1, "better results raise confidence," "confident teachers use it better," "better use improves results"; loop 2, "a faster rollout means more work," "more overload means more resistance," "more resistance slows the rollout"; loop 3, "more initiatives, more fatigue," "more fatigue, less effort on each," "more effort, better results," "better results, fewer new initiatives"; loop 4, "more converts, fewer shrines sold," "fewer sales, more opposition," "more opposition, fewer converts"; loop 5, "honoring the weak deepens belonging," "belonging grows care," "care gives honor to the weak"; loop 6, "more pressure, more fear," "more fear, less practice," "more practice, better results," "better results, less pressure." **Provenance:** Loops 1 and 2 are the worked example in *AI-Native Schools*, Chapter 18, "Sustaining Change: Systems Thinking and National Adoption," repeated in this chapter's section "Systems Thinking." Loop 3 is built from this chapter's section "Change Fatigue"; loop 4 from "The Economics of Resistance" (Acts 19 and Pliny's letter); loop 5 from "One Body, Many Parts" (1 Corinthians 12); loop 6 from "The Implementation Dip." All six are illustrative simplifications, and the sim labels them "Illustrative loops." **Rules:** Type = Reinforcing if the number of minus signs around the loop is even (0, 2, ...) and Balancing if it is odd. Each loop has exactly one correct type, given in Content. A loop is scored on its first submitted answer only. Score counts first-attempt correct answers out of 6. Mastery is score >= 5. Zoom and reset are by buttons; mouse-wheel zoom is disabled. **Learner Activity:** 1. The learner sees loop 1 drawn as a ring with signed arrows, the counting rule, and the two choices. 2. The learner counts the minus signs, selects a type, and submits. The sim marks the answer and shows the "Why" text. 3. If incorrect, the learner may choose again; the second attempt does not change the score, and after it the correct type is shown. 4. The learner moves through all six loops in order. 5. After loop 6, the sim shows the score and a summary of the six loops with their minus-sign counts and types. 6. The learner should notice that four loops are reinforcing and two balancing, that two harmful loops (3 and 6) are reinforcing, and that the Ephesus loop has the same structure as the school rollout loop (2). **Feedback:** Six loops, fixed order, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: [type]. [Why]" Incorrect: "Not quite. Count every minus sign around the whole loop, then check: even or odd?" After the second attempt the correct type and "Why" are shown and the loop counts as missed. A running score "First-try correct: n of 6" is shown. Final message for score >= 5: "You can read a loop, in Ephesus or in a staff room." For score < 5: "Review the counting rule and try the six loops again." A "Try again" option restarts from loop 1. **Starting State:** Loop 1, the counting rule, the score "First-try correct: 0 of 6," and the question "Is this loop reinforcing or balancing?" **Chapter Anchors:** The counting rule (even minus signs is reinforcing, odd is balancing); the two rollout loops from *AI-Native Schools* Chapter 18 (results, confidence, quality of use; rollout speed, overload, resistance); Pliny's letter of about 112 CE; six loops.
